articles.author: rowan-vale
articles.title: Lamb gets 250, Tare gets six, and Saffron gets to work
articles.dek: The Psi Corps close 14–3 with a 49–10 win over Fuchsia, five Archam Manning touchdown passes and no punts.

body.text: HeeDee Lamb caught eight passes for 250 yards and three touchdowns. NeMarcus Tare sacked Empoleon six times. Archam Manning threw five touchdown passes, and Saffron never punted. The Psi Corps finished their regular season with a 49–10 victory over Fuchsia and several excellent reasons to hurry the conversation toward the playoffs. I would nevertheless like to spend a moment with two hundred and fifty receiving yards. The number deserves a chair.

Lamb scored on passes of forty-five, twenty-three and sixty-seven yards. His first two touchdowns went down the left side and built a 14–0 lead before the first quarter ended. The third came on fourth-and-two late in the third quarter, when Manning threw deep right and the Heliolisk supplied a much larger answer than the required distance. Saffron was already ahead 35–3. The offense continued using the space Fuchsia gave it.

Manning completed twenty-seven of thirty-five passes for 436 yards, five touchdowns and one interception. The Psi Corps gained 519 total yards to Fuchsia’s 186, moved the chains twenty-two times and converted five of seven third downs. A regular season that ended with 597 points had one more extensive demonstration to offer. Trent Scarboro’s team now hosts Olivine as the second seed in Kanto–Johto.

The defense contributed its own form of pressure. Tare’s six sacks accounted for all six credited against Empoleon, costing Fuchsia thirty-five yards. He also recovered a fumble after Sharpedo caught a fourteen-yard pass early in the second quarter. Jack Slampert intercepted Empoleon in the first. Fuchsia’s offense had trouble preserving possessions long enough to make the game competitive, and Saffron repeatedly converted those difficulties into another opportunity to score.
Lamb made the long throws worthwhile

Look at how many guys finished something for the next guy. The protection gives Archam a chance, the receivers finish it, the defense gets us back out there. I love that. Now we have to earn the right to do it again.
body.speaker: Trent Scarboro

body.text: The first touchdown arrived at 3:28 of the opening quarter, Manning finding Lamb deep left for forty-five yards. After Slampert’s interception, the same quarterback-receiver combination produced a twenty-three-yard score with eight seconds left in the period. Lamb finished the day with eight receptions on ten targets. He averaged 31.3 yards per catch, a figure that makes ordinary third-down analysis feel slightly underdressed.

Fuchsia could not devote the entire afternoon to him without allowing other work to continue. Mothel Irving caught six passes for seventy-one yards, and Bysson Witten added five for fifty-seven. Manning’s other touchdown throws went to Pawmo from one yard and L’oudre Swift from two. Dam Skattebo scored on a one-yard run and finished with fifty rushing yards on thirteen carries. Emmitt Smoth contributed twenty-seven yards on five.

body.alt: Archam Manning threw five touchdown passes. A conceptual meeting-room still life, not a recorded photograph.
body.caption: Archam Manning threw five touchdown passes. A conceptual meeting-room still life, not a recorded photograph.

body.text: Those shorter scores matter because they show how Saffron completed possessions that did not finish with a long Lamb reception. The Psi Corps could reach the goal line and use several available players. Manning’s five touchdown passes went to three receivers, with Skattebo adding the conventional rushing score. The offense did not require every successful play to be spectacular, even though Lamb made the spectacular ones unusually common.

The sixty-seven-yard touchdown came with fifty-six seconds left in the third quarter. Saffron faced fourth-and-two and attacked deep right. The recorded play ends with Lamb in the end zone, a gain that converted the down and added seven points after the extra point. It was the most emphatic example of a defense being asked to cover both the immediate requirement and the full field. Fuchsia solved neither on that play.
Tare finished a twenty-nine-sack season

Tare’s final total reached twenty-nine sacks, the league lead. Chen Norton Jr finished with twenty-three, giving the Psi Corps fifty-two from those two players alone. The finale belonged overwhelmingly to Tare: a six-yard loss on third-and-nine in the first quarter, a four-yard loss on third-and-one in the second, and two more takedowns late in that half. He kept returning to Empoleon before the Shadows could turn possession into a stable drive.

The sacks also help explain Fuchsia’s modest attempt count. Empoleon completed fifteen of twenty-six for 162 yards, with no passing touchdowns and one interception. The Shadows ran only nine times for twenty-four yards. They converted two of eight third downs and punted five times. Their offense rarely got enough consecutive successful plays to change the scoring requirement facing the next possession.

Saffron did have mistakes. Manning threw an interception late in the first half, and the Psi Corps lost a fumble. Those giveaways did not create a close game because the defense kept making Fuchsia begin again. The final turnover count was two for each team. A reader looking only at that even total would miss the larger difference in sustained offense and the pressure applied to the quarterbacks. Saffron took one sack; Fuchsia took six.

body.alt: Ninetales #42. NeMarcus Tare finished with six sacks against Fuchsia. An imagined warmup portrait.
body.caption: NeMarcus Tare finished with six sacks against Fuchsia. An imagined warmup portrait.

body.text: The Shadows scored on a 57-yard Gorebyss field goal in the third quarter and a three-yard Kricketune run in the fourth. Neither score changed the direction of the afternoon. Between them, Jolt Train Ln returned a punt sixty-six yards for Saffron’s seventh touchdown. The Psi Corps finished with five passing scores, one rushing score and one return score, with all seven extra points successful.

Manning’s scoring distribution also matters beyond Lamb’s spectacular afternoon. Pawmo and Loudre Swift finished the other touchdown passes, while Skattebo scored on the ground and Jolt Train Ln supplied the punt-return touchdown. Seven touchdowns therefore came from passing, rushing and special teams. Fuchsia would have needed to solve several different problems to make the game competitive after the early separation.

The third-down comparison reinforces the offensive control. Saffron converted five of seven and never punted. Twenty-two first downs kept opportunities available, while Fuchsia managed nine. The Psi Corps did turn the ball over twice, matching the Shadows’ two, so the margin cannot be explained by a simple turnover advantage. They repeatedly moved and finished better during the possessions they retained.

Those are useful details for the Olivine preparation because a playoff favorite still has to handle ordinary downs. A long Lamb touchdown can transform a drive; an efficient conversion prevents the offense from needing that rescue. Scarboro has evidence of both from the finale. The next opponent’s injuries increase Saffron’s advantage on paper, but the assignments remain to protect Manning, give the receivers usable throws and prevent a limited offense from receiving unnecessary extra possessions.
The postseason starts with a favorable assignment

Olivine arrives after beating Azalea 17–0 to secure the seventh seed. The Ironclads earned the berth, and their defense has produced useful low-scoring wins. Their current offense has a difficult new problem: Gabite suffered an eight-week injury in the finale after leading the team with 702 rushing yards. Gogoat is also out with four weeks reported. That leaves Drampa facing Saffron’s pressure with less established backfield help.

Saffron has no positive-week injury entries in the current report. That is an advantage to discuss concretely, particularly when several other contenders are replacing important offensive players. It gives Scarboro the same available core that just produced this finale. It does not guarantee another forty-nine points or six sacks. Olivine’s plan will be to make the game slower, cleaner and considerably less generous to Lamb downfield.

The Psi Corps finished 14–3. Their three defeats came by one point at Vermilion and three points each at Mossdeep and Mt. Silver. That record presents a clear postseason assignment: keep the broad production, then finish the close games against the strongest opponents. Saffron has already shown it can score enough to compete with both first seeds. Winning four consecutive playoff games requires more than remembering that the losses were narrow.

Manning ended as the league’s passing-yardage leader at 4,633. Lamb finished with 1,878 receiving yards and eighteen receiving touchdowns. Skattebo reached 1,026 rushing yards and eighteen rushing touchdowns. Those are substantial individual seasons that fit together into the league’s second-highest scoring total. The first playoff opponent must defend the whole combination, with Tare and Norton waiting when possession changes.

Scarboro can take considerable confidence from the finale while correcting the two giveaways. The Psi Corps scored on long throws, short throws, a short run and a punt return; they kept their own punter out of the game and repeatedly put Fuchsia’s on the field. That is a useful closing performance. Olivine now gets the first opportunity to make Saffron’s January ambitions require a less comfortable kind of football.

art.alt: Heliolisk #11. HeeDee Lamb caught three touchdown passes and gained 250 receiving yards. An editorial receiving illustration.

articles.author: dorian-pike
articles.title: Crobat takes three touchdowns out of Mt. Silver’s finale
articles.dek: Cianwood wins 21–13 behind a 98-yard return and two receiving scores; the Reds enter their bye with more injuries and no second-half points.

body.text: Crobat scored all three Cianwood touchdowns, and Mt. Silver spent the second half unable to produce a reply. The Crushers won 21–13, finishing their season 8–9 with a victory over the conference’s first seed. The Reds finished 14–3 and retained their bye. They also finished with two more players carrying multiweek injuries, which makes the extra round of rest useful in a way nobody needs to explain with a slogan.

The first Crobat touchdown answered Mt. Silver’s opening score immediately. Garshawn Lynch had just run right for five yards and a touchdown with 2:08 left in the first quarter. Weepinbell made the extra point, then kicked off. Crobat returned it ninety-eight yards. Cianwood was level before the Reds’ defense had been asked to protect the lead on an ordinary possession.

The next two scores came through the passing game. Gardevoir hit Crobat deep through the middle for fifty yards with 2:55 left in the third quarter. Near the end of the same period, a short pass left became an eleven-yard touchdown. Cianwood moved from a 13–7 halftime deficit to a 21–13 lead, then kept Mt. Silver from scoring in the fourth.

Crobat caught all four of his targets for 107 yards and two touchdowns, adding 119 yards on two returns, one of them the ninety-eight-yard score. It is a tidy way to dominate an afternoon: catch every intended pass, score twice through the air and answer the opponent’s first touchdown before its supporters have settled back into their seats. Cianwood did not need a huge passing volume because so much of the useful work reached the same player.
Lynch gave Mt. Silver a lead worth keeping
We gave him the return, then let him catch the other two. Very hospitable of us. We have a week to become less welcoming.
body.speaker: Connor McLarren

body.text: Lynch carried eleven times for eighty-eight yards and the touchdown, averaging eight yards per attempt. His longest run gained thirty-one. Rat Grange added twenty-four yards on four carries, and Vibrava had four yards on three. The Reds finished with 116 rushing yards and 276 total yards, more than Cianwood’s 235. Their problem was converting enough of that movement into points after halftime.

Crem Ftzpatrik completed twenty-three of thirty-five passes for 160 yards, without a touchdown or interception. The available passing game leaned heavily on shorter completions. Vulpix caught ten passes for sixty yards on seventeen targets. Doduo gained sixty-three yards on four catches, and Bayleef added fifteen on three. Those receptions kept parts of the offense functioning, but the final score required an explosive answer or another finished drive that never arrived.

body.alt: Garchomp #22. Garshawn Lynch rushed for eighty-eight yards and a touchdown. An imagined practice portrait.
body.caption: Garshawn Lynch rushed for eighty-eight yards and a touchdown. An imagined practice portrait.

body.text: Weepinbell made field goals from thirty-four and forty-two yards in the second quarter. Those kicks restored the lead after Crobat’s return touchdown and sent Mt. Silver to halftime ahead 13–7. The Reds had produced a touchdown and two successful field-goal possessions. They had also avoided turnovers. There was a workable game available if the second half could preserve enough of that offense.

Instead, Mt. Silver finished two of eleven on third down and punted five times. Cianwood also punted five times, but its scoring opportunities produced three touchdowns when the return is included. The difference between an offense that moved the ball and one that completed the required scoring work was decisive. The Reds did not lose this game because the box score refused to acknowledge their yards. They lost because Crobat’s touchdowns required a larger answer than thirteen points.
Cianwood closed without giving the ball away

Gardevoir completed eleven of sixteen passes for 144 yards and two touchdowns, taking one sack and throwing no interceptions. The Crushers had no lost fumbles either. Their twenty-three rushing attempts produced ninety-one yards, and that work helped keep the offense from demanding a pass on every useful down. Doduo led the runners with thirty-nine yards on ten carries, while Bibarel gained thirty-one on five.

The closing possession showed the value of ordinary gains after the dramatic ones. With two minutes left, Mankey ran for three yards on second-and-seven, then seven on third-and-four. Gardevoir completed a short pass to him, and Wigglytuff added a ten-yard run. The Crushers reached the kneel-downs without giving Mt. Silver the possession it needed to attempt a late tie.

That sequence belongs beside Crobat’s three scores. A team that has built an eight-point advantage still has to protect the ball and end the game. Cianwood did so with a converted third down and enough additional movement to consume the remaining time. Chuck’s club finished with a victory that required both explosive production and careful closing work.

body.alt: Alcremie #12. Crem Ftzpatrik threw for 160 yards in the loss. An imagined sideline portrait.
body.caption: Crem Ftzpatrik threw for 160 yards in the loss. An imagined sideline portrait.

body.text: The result could not get Cianwood into the playoffs because Olivine won at Azalea and took the final Kanto–Johto berth. The Crushers finish 8–9, with consecutive wins over Olivine and Mt. Silver. Their broader offseason assessment can wait. This finale gives them a concrete achievement: they beat a fourteen-win team on the road and completed the fourth quarter without allowing it another score.

The five punts on each side reveal how much the scoring plays mattered. Cianwood did not sustain a relentless stream of successful possessions, and Mt. Silver was not repeatedly handing over turnovers. The Crushers needed the return and the two touchdown catches to turn a modest offensive afternoon into twenty-one points. The Reds needed one more finishing possession after halftime and never produced it.

Lynch’s early touchdown had offered a more comfortable possibility. With an established running contribution and a lead, Mt. Silver could have made Cianwood answer a series of longer offensive assignments. Crobat’s immediate return removed that opportunity. The Reds still reached halftime ahead through two Weepinbell field goals, but each field goal left the opponent close enough for one successful touchdown drive to change the game.

McLarren’s next preparation therefore has two distinct subjects. The offense must identify how to finish drives with its available passing personnel, and the coverage units must prevent a score of their own from being answered before the defense gets a snap. Neither correction requires dismissing the fourteen wins that earned the bye. Both come directly from a final game in which an opponent with no remaining margin in its playoff pursuit played well enough to win.
The bye has immediate personnel value

Mt. Silver’s current report lists Vibrava out five weeks and Medicham four after the finale. Those injuries join an already consequential group: Tic Thorpe has three weeks reported, Josh Alakazam four, Tony Gyarzalez five and Ariados ten. Ninji Asomugha has one. These are recovery durations in the current report, not guarantees about the lineup in a particular future round.

Connor McLarren has to prepare the available offense first. Lynch’s 1,200 rushing yards led the league, and the finale showed he remains capable of productive work. Ftzpatrik protected the ball, but the passing game produced 160 yards on thirty-five attempts and no touchdowns. The missing quarterbacks and receiving options make it necessary to choose a practical route to points rather than describe the roster as though everyone is about to return together.

The Reds still own the first seed. They will host the lowest surviving Kanto–Johto team after the wild-card round, and they need three wins for the championship. That advantage was earned across fourteen victories, including a 36–33 win over Saffron. It survives this loss. So does the evidence from the 38–24 defeat at Cinnabar two weeks earlier, another game in which the opponent reached a score Mt. Silver could not match.

I still see a team capable of winning the conference, particularly if Lynch can keep the available passing offense in useful situations. I also see a finale that makes the conditions of that claim more demanding. The coverage must avoid another return touchdown. The offense must convert more than two third downs. The defense must prevent one receiver from deciding the game in three separate ways.

McLarren has a bye in which to make those corrections and learn which players can contribute. Crobat has a finale with two receiving touchdowns and a return score, all earned against the conference’s top seed. The Crushers leave with the victory. The Reds keep the home-field route and a clear set of problems to solve before anyone comes to use it.

art.alt: Crobat #11. Cianwood’s Crobat returned a kickoff ninety-eight yards for a touchdown. Illustrated from the recorded play.

articles.author: mara-voss
articles.title: Dewford finds the last answer in a 35–29 race
articles.dek: Meowscarada scores on a 99-yard kickoff return and the go-ahead reception; a late Rustboro fumble ends the Stone’s best response.

body.text: Rustboro took a 29–28 lead at the start of the fourth quarter and then allowed the exact kind of answer it could least afford. Frosmoth found Meowscarada deep right for a touchdown at 4:39. Dewford had its lead back, and Rustboro’s next promising completion ended with the ball belonging to the Breakers.

Gibby Timmy caught a thirty-five-yard pass from Shawn Watzon at 4:08, then fumbled. Thievul recovered for Dewford. The Stone had already answered several scores with productive offense, but that turnover removed their most immediate chance to do it again. Dewford finished the game with an eleven-win record and the fifth seed. Rustboro finished 9–8 and sixth, with a trip to Petalburg waiting.

Meowscarada supplied two very different touchdowns. The first was a ninety-nine-yard kickoff return immediately after Rustboro tied the game 7–7. The second restored Dewford’s lead in the fourth quarter. The receiver caught four passes for 127 yards and added 131 return yards on two attempts. A defense and a coverage unit both had an opportunity to prevent a decisive score, and neither did enough.

The final totals were close in ways that do little to soften the specific failures. Rustboro gained 380 yards to Dewford’s 370. Neither quarterback threw an interception or took a sack. The Breakers committed no turnovers; the Stone lost the one fumble. Dewford also converted eight of eleven third downs, keeping its offense on the field for fifty-six plays compared with Rustboro’s thirty-four.
The scoring began before either defense settled

If you let somebody stay at your house for fifty-six plays, they will eventually start rearranging the furniture. We had thirty-four. Some of ours were excellent. We needed to make them leave more often.
body.speaker: Tyler Scarboro

body.text: Dewford’s Watchog scored on a one-yard run with 2:45 left in the first quarter. Rustboro answered on fourth-and-one, its own Watchog running up the middle for sixteen yards and a touchdown. That was a successful decision to pursue the first down and more. It also lasted as a tied score for only the time required to kick off, because Meowscarada returned the ensuing kick ninety-nine yards.

Philly Gabite tied the game again on a six-yard run at the start of the second quarter. The Breakers then used a thirty-yard Frosmoth pass to Swellow to move ahead 21–14. Rustboro’s next answer came late in the half, Watzon finding Gibby Timmy short right for a twenty-yard touchdown on third-and-eleven. The teams went to halftime level at twenty-one after repeatedly completing the most important parts of their drives.

body.alt: Archeops #99. Gibby Timmy caught five passes for 148 yards and a touchdown. An editorial receiving collage.
body.caption: Gibby Timmy caught five passes for 148 yards and a touchdown. An editorial receiving collage.

body.text: Those sequences gave the Stone reasons to believe their offense could win the game. Watzon finished fifteen of twenty-one for 296 yards, a touchdown and no interceptions. Timmy caught five of six targets for 148 yards and the score. Philly Gabite added fifty-eight receiving yards on four catches alongside forty-two rushing yards and his touchdown. Rustboro had several ways to move the ball quickly.

The issue was how often it would be allowed to try. Dewford’s running game and third-down conversions kept producing new sets of downs. Excadrill carried twenty-two times for 101 yards and a touchdown, with Watchog adding twenty-nine yards and a score on eight carries. The Breakers ran thirty-nine times for 149 yards. Their larger play count was earned through successful possession work, not simply given to them by a passive opponent.
Rustboro took the lead, then lost the possession it needed

Excadrill’s seven-yard run put Dewford ahead 28–21 in the third quarter. Rustboro answered at the beginning of the fourth with Watchog’s four-yard touchdown run. Tyler Scarboro chose a two-point attempt, and Watzon completed a short pass left to Huntail. The Stone led 29–28. Their offense had completed another response and placed the requirement back on Dewford.

Frosmoth met it on third-and-seven with the deep throw to Meowscarada. The Breakers’ quarterback attempted only seventeen passes, completing ten for 221 yards and two touchdowns. The modest completion count did not prevent the passing game from being decisive. Swellow’s earlier thirty-yard score and Meowscarada’s fourth-quarter touchdown supplied large gains at moments when Dewford needed to finish.

Timmy’s fumble came on the following Rustboro possession. The thirty-five-yard completion itself demonstrated the same attacking ability that had kept the Stone involved. Losing the ball after it turned a promising answer into a defensive assignment. The record credits Thievul with the recovery; it does not support inventing an individual coverage or ball-security explanation beyond the play that was actually recorded.

body.alt: Frosmoth #12. Dewford’s Frosmoth threw two touchdown passes. An imagined sideline portrait.
body.caption: Dewford’s Frosmoth threw two touchdown passes. An imagined sideline portrait.

body.text: The Breakers still had to close. Near the two-minute warning, Watchog gained nine yards on second-and-ten after being held to no gain on first down. Dewford’s ability to keep demanding another tackle had been useful throughout the game. It became particularly valuable when Rustboro needed possession more urgently than another small statistical improvement on defense.

Rustboro’s thirteen rushing attempts also left the shape of its offense exposed. The Stone generated eighty-four yards from those carries, so the ground game was productive when used. Dewford ran thirty-nine times for 149 yards and converted far more third downs, giving its offense fifty-six plays against Rustboro’s thirty-four. Explosive receiving gains allowed the Stone to keep scoring with fewer snaps, but they did not give the defense the same amount of time between assignments.

That does not mean a losing team should simply copy the winner’s play count. Rustboro’s passing efficiency was a strength: fifteen completions on twenty-one attempts produced 296 yards without an interception. The problem was that the game demanded another useful possession after the late lead disappeared. Timmy’s fumble ended a promising gain at the moment the Stone most needed to preserve the ball and complete the answer.

The next opponent makes that lesson immediate. Petalburg has already beaten Rustboro twice and is comfortable keeping the total lower than this game’s sixty-four combined points. The Stone cannot count on another offensive exchange with room for repeated repairs. Watzon’s clean interception column and Timmy’s big catches offer a plausible route forward, provided the next scoring opportunity survives the end of the catch.
Dewford’s available offense reaches Eterna in good form

The Breakers have now won three straight, beating Oreburgh, Mauville and Rustboro. They finished with 328 points scored and 288 allowed. Their opening playoff opponent, Eterna, allowed only 184 points but enters with several important offensive absences. Dewford has no positive-week injury entries in the current report. That gives Brawly a healthier available group to take into a road game that is likely to demand more patience than this finale did.

The return touchdown is a major part of the score, so it should not be assumed to repeat. The offensive touchdown drives are stronger evidence for what Dewford can attempt again: a productive running game, enough third-down conversions and a passing game capable of finding the larger gain. Frosmoth does not need thirty completions to matter if the throws he does complete move a possession into scoring range or finish it.

Rustboro has a different problem to solve at Petalburg. The Pride beat the Stone 30–7 and 17–10 in the regular season. Their leading runner, Oinkologne, remains unavailable, which creates an opening for a better Rustboro result. The Stone cannot make full use of that opportunity if their defense allows another opponent to convert eight of eleven third downs. This finale showed offensive capacity alongside the cost of repeatedly having to answer.

Smoke Break recorded four tackles for loss for Rustboro, concrete defensive successes within an afternoon that still allowed thirty-five points. That combination is worth understanding. A defense can win several snaps and fail to end enough possessions. The Breakers had the running volume and third-down execution to survive their losses and continue working toward the next score.

Scarboro’s offense finished with twenty-nine points, three rushing touchdowns and a successful two-point conversion. The work was substantial. The kickoff return, the late deep touchdown and the fumble explain why it was insufficient. Rustboro now gets a playoff game in which the offensive standard should remain ambitious and the defensive requirement needs to become much more reliable.

art.alt: Meowscarada #21. Meowscarada returned a kickoff ninety-nine yards for a touchdown. Illustrated from the recorded play.

articles.author: tessa-wren
articles.title: Sunyshore runs for 213, then turns to an injury-shaped playoff week
articles.dek: The Starseekers win 23–3 and finish 13–4, but 88 Special’s sixteen-week injury entry changes the preparation for Hearthome.

body.text: Sunyshore’s defense scored first, its running game supplied most of the offensive movement, and its injury report became the most consequential item carried out of a 23–3 win at Veilstone. The Starseekers finished 13–4 and secured the second seed in Hoenn–Sinnoh. They will host Hearthome in the wild-card round after beating the Haunts twice during the season. They will prepare for that third meeting with 88 Special listed out sixteen weeks.

The receiver caught two passes for twenty-six yards and returned two kicks for forty-seven in the finale. The game record confirms participation and the injury report confirms the absence; it does not provide a reliable injury timestamp or medical diagnosis. Karson Jones now has to redistribute the available receiving work. That is a practical adjustment for a team whose broader performance at Veilstone was convincing.

Myles Gabite carried sixteen times for 110 yards and a touchdown. FLOAT SZN added ninety-four yards and a touchdown on seven carries, including a fifty-two-yard gain and the thirteen-yard scoring run that finished Sunyshore’s points late in the fourth quarter. The Starseekers rushed twenty-eight times for 213 yards. Veilstone ran nineteen times for forty-three.

That difference gave the visitors control despite three giveaways. DeZhaun Watzon threw one interception, and Sunyshore lost two fumbles. Its defense held Veilstone to ninety-five total yards, five first downs and one successful third down in ten attempts. The Starseekers did enough ordinary defensive work to prevent the turnovers from producing a competitive score.
Whirler put the defense on the scoreboard
We earned a home playoff game. That stadium should feel it. And every player in our room needs to understand that the opportunity just got bigger for somebody. We are going to prepare him for it.
body.speaker: Karson Jones

body.text: The opening points came with 4:24 remaining in the first quarter. Veilstone faced third-and-ten, and Whiscash ran right for a two-yard loss, with Fred Whirler making the tackle for a safety. Sunyshore led 2–0. The play established a defensive advantage that continued through the rest of the game: the Fists struggled to create room for productive possessions even when they received an extra opportunity.

Veilstone quarterback Tatsugiri completed nine of eighteen passes for fifty-two yards, throwing one interception and taking one sack. Seviper caught six passes for forty yards. The rest of the receiving group contributed very little yardage. Whiscash’s sixteen carries produced thirty-eight yards, and Palpitoad added five on three. Sunyshore did not need repeated sacks to restrict the offense; it kept successful gains scarce across several kinds of play.

body.alt: Poliwrath #56. Fred Whirler recorded the opening safety. An editorial defensive illustration.
body.caption: Fred Whirler recorded the opening safety. An editorial defensive illustration.

body.text: Conkel Jones and Whirler each recorded six tackles. Serp Gardener had four and a tackle for loss. Vig Rothington supplied the sack, and Parasect intercepted Tatsugiri late in the fourth quarter. Those contributions came from different parts of the available defense. The unit’s effectiveness was broader than the safety that placed the first points on the scoreboard.

Veilstone’s only score was a 53-yard Sunflora field goal with 5:18 left in the fourth quarter. Sunyshore had already built a 16–0 lead. The Fists had taken possession after an interception, but the drive still ended in a long kick rather than a touchdown. That was a recurring feature of the afternoon: opportunities existed, and the Starseekers’ defense kept reducing their value.
The running game finished what the early safety began

Myles Gabite scored on a one-yard run with 3:11 left in the second quarter. The extra point made it 9–0. Sunyshore then added a seven-yard Watzon pass through the middle to Jolt Vick with seventeen seconds left before halftime, extending the lead to 16–0. The offense had combined a short rushing finish with a short passing finish after the defense supplied the initial two points.

Watzon finished sixteen of twenty-three for 158 yards, one touchdown and one interception. MF STOMP caught all seven of his targets for sixty-seven yards, giving the quarterback a reliable source of completions. Fera LaGatr added three catches for twenty-five, while 88 Special contributed the two for twenty-six. The passing game did not have to carry the full yardage requirement because the runners were already producing substantial gains.

FLOAT SZN’s late touchdown arrived at 1:58 of the fourth, a thirteen-yard run through the middle. It followed a productive rushing sequence that included work by Myles Gabite. The score made it 23–3 and left Veilstone with a large deficit and little time. The Starseekers finished with sixteen first downs and converted five of nine third downs.

body.alt: Porygon-Z #30. DeZhaun Watzon threw for 158 yards and a touchdown. An editorial passing illustration.
body.caption: DeZhaun Watzon threw for 158 yards and a touchdown. An editorial passing illustration.

body.text: Their ball security still deserves specific attention. MF STOMP fumbled after a four-yard reception in the third quarter, and Jolt Vick lost the ball after a seven-yard catch in the fourth. Watzon’s interception came between those events. Sunyshore had the defensive performance to survive all three. A playoff opponent may be better equipped to turn the same opportunities into touchdowns.

Sunyshore’s three turnovers give Jones a concrete reason to keep the meeting demanding after a comfortable score. The defense limited the resulting damage to a single field goal, but the offense cannot build its playoff plan around receiving that protection every time. A 23–3 win can contain both strong rushing execution and possessions that were unnecessarily lost.

Veilstone’s third-down difficulty kept those openings from becoming a sustained comeback. The Fists converted one of ten, while Sunyshore converted five of nine. The home offense therefore struggled to remain on the field long enough to exploit the extra chances. The Starseekers could regain possession and return to a running game that had already supplied a reliable source of yardage.

The finale also gave Jones a useful example of scoring responsibility beyond the injured receiver. Myles Gabite supplied the largest rushing workload, FLOAT SZN produced the late touchdown, and Jolt Vick caught the touchdown pass. MF STOMP’s seven catches provided repeated receiving help. Those contributions are specific evidence for the next preparation, even though they do not establish how the playoff targets or carries will be allocated. Hearthome must prepare for the available offense Sunyshore actually showed, while Jones must decide how to make it more careful with the ball.
The third Hearthome meeting begins with new evidence

The Starseekers won 28–3 at home against Hearthome in Week 1 and 53–17 on the road in Week 13. Those results provide direct matchup evidence and a clear reason to favor Sunyshore. The Haunts have also won five straight since the second defeat, finishing 8–8–1 and claiming the seventh seed. The next game should account for that improvement rather than treat the earlier margin as a fixed property of the matchup.

The loss of 88 Special is the major new personnel fact for Jones. The current injury duration is sixteen weeks. There is no need to invent a diagnosis or an exact recovery date to explain the effect: a player who caught passes and returned kicks in the finale is unavailable for the immediate assignment. Fera LaGatr, Jolt Vick and the other available options will have to carry the receiving work that remains.

The running game gives Sunyshore a useful way to support that adjustment. Myles Gabite and FLOAT SZN combined for 204 rushing yards at Veilstone. Their season totals were 499 and 566 respectively, reflecting a group with more than one productive back. Repeating the finale’s efficiency against a playoff defense is uncertain, but the actual performance gives Jones a concrete part of the offense to build around.

Sunyshore finished with 423 points scored and 211 allowed. Its losses at Eterna, 14–6, and Mossdeep, 27–3, show how better defenses have limited it. Its last two wins, 34–7 at Pastoria and 23–3 at Veilstone, show a team closing with defensive control. The first playoff game asks the Starseekers to combine that defense with cleaner possession management and a revised receiving plan.

Jones has thirteen wins, a home game and two earlier victories over the opponent. He also has three turnovers to correct and a consequential receiver to replace. The finale supplied confidence through the running game and defense, then made the next week’s preparation more demanding. Sunyshore’s route remains promising, with the available offense now required to demonstrate how much of its success can travel beyond the missing player.
